result.topic_en: Euler shows that the n-th differences of the sequence of n-th powers equal n!, so not all of 1^n−1, 2^n−1, ..., n^n−1 can be divisible by a prime 2p+1 when n<2p, and then discusses when a^p−1 is divisible by primes of the form 6p+1 and 4p+1.
result.transcription:
32 \quad L. EULERI OPERA POSTHUMA. \quad Arithmetica.

257. Qui enim hoc negaverit, affirmare debet omnes has formulas $1^n-1$, $2^n-1$, $3^n-1$, $4^n-1$, $5^n-1,\ldots n^n-1$ per $2p+1$ esse divisibiles, ideoque etiam earum differentias tam primas $2^n-1$, $3^n-2^n$, $4^n-3^n$, $5^n-4^n$, etc. quam secundas $3^n-2.2^n+1^n$, $4^n-2\,3^n+2^n$, $5^n-2.4^n+3^n$, etc. et sequentes omnes.

258. Differentiae autem ordine $n$ sunt constantes, quae si littera $N$ indicentur, ita exprimuntur ut sit $N=(n+1)^n-n.n^n+\frac{n(n-1)}{1.2}(n-1)^n-\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{1.2.3}(n-2)^n+$ etc. cujus expressionis valores pro variis valoribus ipsius $n$ facile colliguntur:
Si $n=1$ est $N=2-1=1$
$n=2$ \quad $N=3^2-2.2^2+1=2=1.2$
$n=3$ \quad $N=4^3-3.3^3+3.2^3-1=6=1.2.3$
$n=4$ \quad $N=5^4-4.4^4+6.3^4-4.2^4+1=24=1.2.3.4$
etc.

259. Ad quod clarius ostendendum sit, pro $n$ scribendo $n+1$,
$P=(n+2)^{n+1}-(n+1)(n+1)^{n+1}+\frac{(n+1)n}{1.2}n^{n+1}-\frac{(n+1)n(n-1)}{1.2.3}(n-1)^{n+1}+$ etc.
et a termino anteriori incipiendo
$P=(n+1)^{n+1}-(n+1)n^{n+1}+\frac{(n+1)n}{1.2}(n-1)^{n+1}-$ etc.
At valor ipsius $N$ ita repraesentari potest
$N=(n+1)^n-n^{n+1}+\frac{n}{1.2}(n-1)^{n+1}-\frac{n(n-1)}{1.2.3}(n-2)^{n+1}+$ etc.
quae per $n+1$ multiplicata praebet valorem ipsius $P$, ita ut sit $P=(n+1)N$.

260. Cum igitur casu $n=1$ sit $N=1$, casu $n=2$ erit $N=1.2$, casu $n=3$ erit $N=1.2.3$, et in genere pro numero quocunque $n$ erit $N=1.2.3\ldots n$. At haec differentia ordinis $n$ non est divisibilis per numerum primum $2p+1$, ob $n<2p$, unde sequitur non omnes terminos seriei § 257 expositae per eum esse divisibiles.

261. Sit $6p+1$ numerus primus, et cum forma $a^{6p}-1$ per eum sit divisibilis, nisi $a$ ejus sit multiplum, dabuntur casus, quibus etiam $a^p-1$ per eum dividi poterit, scilicet sumto $a=e^3\pm\lambda(6p+1)$. Tum vero etiam dantur casus, quibus formula $a^{2p}-1$ non erit divisibilis per istum numerum primum $6p+1$, uti ex demonstratione modo allata patet.

262. Cum ante ostenderimus formulam $a^{3p}-1$ fore per $6p+1$ divisibilem, si fuerit
$a=cc\pm\lambda(6p+1)$,
nunc colligere licet, si numerus $a$ simul in hac forma $cc\pm\lambda(6p+1)$ et in hac $c^3\pm\lambda(6p+1)$ contineatur, tum etiam formulam $a^p-1$ per $6p+1$ fore divisibilem, id quod quoque continget si fuerit $a=c^6\pm\lambda(6p+1)$.

263. Si sit $4p+1$ numerus primus, ut $a^{4p}-1$ per eum sit divisibile, tum adeo $a^p-1$ per eum dividi poterit, si fuerit $a=c^4\pm\lambda(4p+1)$. Dantur vero etiam casus, quibus formula $a^p-1$ divisionem non admittet: iis ergo vel $a^p+1$, vel $a^{2p}+1$ certe per $4p+1$ erit divisibile.

methods.what: n-th finite difference of the sequence k^n is the constant n!
Inductive step: the (n+1)-th difference P equals (n+1) times N
methods.quote: quae per $n+1$ multiplicata praebet valorem ipsius $P$, ita ut sit $P=(n+1)N$.

methods.what: Sixth-power residues (both square and cube) mod 6p+1 satisfy a^p ≡ 1
methods.quote: id quod quoque continget si fuerit $a=c^6\pm\lambda(6p+1)$

methods.what: Fourth-power residues mod 4p+1 satisfy a^p ≡ 1; otherwise a^p+1 or a^{2p}+1 divisible
methods.quote: tum adeo $a^p-1$ per eum dividi poterit, si fuerit $a=c^4\pm\lambda(4p+1)$. Dantur vero etiam casus, quibus formula $a^p-1$ divisionem non admittet: iis ergo vel $a^p+1$, vel $a^{2p}+1$ certe per $4p+1$ erit divisibile.

items.quote: Tum vero etiam dantur casus, quibus formula $a^{2p}-1$ non erit divisibilis per istum numerum primum $6p+1$, uti ex demonstratione modo allata patet.
items.english: But there are also cases in which the formula a^{2p}−1 will not be divisible by this prime 6p+1, as is clear from the proof just given.

items.quote: Dantur vero etiam casus, quibus formula $a^p-1$ divisionem non admittet: iis ergo vel $a^p+1$, vel $a^{2p}+1$ certe per $4p+1$ erit divisibile.
items.english: But there are also cases in which the formula a^p−1 will not admit division; in these, therefore, either a^p+1 or a^{2p}+1 will certainly be divisible by 4p+1.
